home.meta1: A speaking head: type IPA or a word and watch a simulated vocal tract say it, in ten languages, voices, tempos and accents.
home.p2: Click an IPA symbol, watch a vocal tract move, hear what comes out.
home.seealso: See also: Pink Trombone by Neil Thapen, the browser vocal-tract synthesizer that started this.
d01.meta1: Drag across the IPA vowel chart and watch a vocal tract make the vowel.
d01.p2: The chart is a map of the tongue: left is front, right is back, top is close to the roof of the mouth, bottom is open. Where two symbols share a spot, the right one has rounded lips. The dot is where your pointer is; on the right, the vocal tract takes the shape that position asks for.
d01.p3: Keyboard and touch friendly: hold any of these.
d02.meta1: Press a symbol in the IPA consonant table and watch the vocal tract close, hiss, buzz or flutter.
d02.p2: Columns are where the tract is narrowed, rows are how. Where a cell has two symbols, the first is voiceless and the second voiced. Stops, affricates, taps and trills are gestures that play through. On the right the tract shows the constriction as it moves.
d03.meta1: Type IPA and hear a vocal tract say it, with the tongue gliding between vowels through the consonants.
d03.p2: Vowels from Demo 1 and consonants from Demo 2, joined by one rule: the tongue leaves the last vowel and arrives at the next while the consonant is made. Stress marks (ˈ ˌ), length (ː), aspiration (ʰ), nasalisation and spaces are understood.
d03.p4: Click a symbol to hear it alone, or to add it at the end.
d04.meta1: Pick a language, type words, see the IPA from a dictionary, and hear a vocal tract say them.
d04.p2: Ten languages, each with a small hand-made dictionary in data/dictionaries. Spanish and Indonesian also have spelling rules, so words outside the dictionary still work. Everything else says which words it does not know. These are seed dictionaries: a pull request adds more.
d05.meta1: The same IPA said by a bass, a child, a soprano, a whisper and more: tract length, pitch and voice quality.
d05.p2: A voice is a tract length, a pitch and a voice quality. A shorter tract moves every resonance up together, which is most of what makes a child sound like a child. Pick a preset and then bend its numbers.
d06.meta1: Speak faster or slower without turning to mush: vowels shorten more than consonants, and fast vowels undershoot.
d06.p2: Real speakers shorten vowels a lot and consonants a little, because a consonant has a physical job to do. Fast vowels also fall short of their targets. Compare the two ways of going fast: speech-like and naive, which squeezes the whole score evenly.
d06.p3: Wider = longer. Purple: vowels. Grey: consonants. Watch how the grey stays wide when the purple shrinks.
d07.meta1: Stress-timed versus syllable-timed speech: same IPA, different clock.
d07.p2: In a syllable-timed language every syllable takes about the same time. In a stress-timed language the stressed syllables are the beats, and the syllables between them are squeezed to fit, which is also why unstressed vowels shrink to ə. Real languages only lean one way. Here you choose.
d07.p3: Each box is a syllable, as wide as it lasts. Purple boxes are stressed. In syllable-timed speech the boxes are the same width; in stress-timed speech the purple ones recur at an even beat.
d08.meta1: Accents as rewrite rules on IPA: edit the rules, hear the same sentence in a different accent.
d08.p2: An accent here is a short list of rewrite rules applied to the IPA before it is sounded. θ > s turns every θ into s; t > ʔ / V _ V does it between vowels only. Pick an accent, then edit its rules and hear the difference. These are sketches of tendencies, not portraits of real people.
d08.label1: English text (words from the dictionary) or IPA between slashes, e.g. /ˈhɛloʊ/

nm.1: clicks, implosives and ejectives (non-pulmonic): they need air from somewhere other than the lungs
nm.2: laterals are approximated: a real lateral lets air round the sides of the tongue, and a tube has no sides, so the midline is narrowed instead
nm.3: voiceless nasals, voiceless approximants and other voiceless versions of voiced symbols: apply voicing off in Demo 3 with the diacritic

demo.1.1.title: Front to back
demo.1.1.blurb: The tongue held high with the lips spread: slide it from front to back (i ɨ ɯ).
lesson.1.1.intro: Only one thing moves. The tongue stays as high as it goes and the lips stay spread; slide the dot from the front (i) through the middle (ɨ) to the back (ɯ) and watch the hump of the tongue travel.
demo.1.2.title: Rounded lips
demo.1.2.blurb: The same height with the lips rounded (y ʉ u): only the lips change.
lesson.1.2.intro: The same height and the same sliding, with the lips rounded (y ʉ u). Compare each with its partner in 1.1: the tongue is in the same place, only the lips changed.
demo.1.3.title: Spread vowels
demo.1.3.blurb: Every vowel with spread lips: move the tongue forward and back, up and down.
lesson.1.3.intro: Now the height is free too. All of these vowels have spread lips: drag anywhere to move the tongue forward and back and up and down.
demo.1.4.title: Rounded vowels
demo.1.4.blurb: Every vowel with rounded lips: move the tongue forward and back, up and down.
lesson.1.4.intro: The same two freedoms with the lips held rounded: the vowels that sit on the right of each pair on the full chart.
demo.2.1.title: Voiceless fricatives
demo.2.1.blurb: A hiss with the voice off. Slide the narrowing from the lips to the throat.
lesson.2.1.intro: A hiss made by pushing air through a narrow gap, with the voice off. Only the place changes: press the line and slide from the lips (ɸ f) through the teeth and ridge (θ s ʃ) to the back of the mouth (x χ) and the throat (ħ).
demo.2.2.title: Voiced fricatives
demo.2.2.blurb: The same hiss with the voice on.
lesson.2.2.intro: The same gaps with the voice on: a buzz under the hiss. Slide along the line and compare each place with its voiceless partner in 2.1.
demo.2.3.title: Voiceless stops
demo.2.3.blurb: A closure and a burst, voice off. Choose where it is made.
lesson.2.3.intro: A stop closes the tract completely and lets go with a burst. Only the place changes: lips (p), ridge (t), palate (c), soft palate (k), uvula (q). Slide to choose a place and let go to hear it.
demo.2.4.title: Voiced stops
demo.2.4.blurb: The same closure and burst with the voice on.
lesson.2.4.intro: The same closures with the voice on: a faint buzz during the closure, then the burst. Slide to choose the place and let go; compare with 2.3.
demo.2.5.title: Nasals
demo.2.5.blurb: The mouth closed at any place, the air going out through the nose.
lesson.2.5.intro: The mouth is closed at some place and the air goes out through the nose. The place of the closure decides which nasal it is: m, n, ŋ, and every one in between.
demo.2.6.title: Approximants
demo.2.6.blurb: A narrowing too wide to hiss: it only colours the voice.
lesson.2.6.intro: A narrowing too wide to hiss: it only colours the voice, like a squeezed vowel. Slide it from the lips (ʋ w) to the palate (j) and the back of the tongue (ɰ).
demo.2.7.title: Laterals
demo.2.7.blurb: The air goes round the sides of the tongue.
lesson.2.7.intro: The air goes round the sides of the tongue. A tube has no sides, so the model narrows the middle instead, the nearest it can come. Choose the kind with the buttons, then slide.
demo.2.8.title: Trills and taps
demo.2.8.blurb: A flutter, or a single flick, of the lips or the tongue.
lesson.2.8.intro: A trill is a flutter of the lips, the tongue tip or the uvula; a tap is one quick flick. Choose which with the buttons, then slide to choose where.
demo.2.9.title: Affricates
demo.2.9.blurb: A stop released into a fricative.
lesson.2.9.intro: A stop released into a fricative: the closure of 2.3 followed by the hiss of 2.1. Slide to choose where it is made.
lesson.axis.hint: Press the line and slide. Hold a symbol to hear exactly that one.
